title: Strong Hearts, Strong Communities
text:
Cardiovascular Health Burden in the United States


Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains one of the most significant public health challenges in the United States. It includes conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels, such as coronary artery disease, heart failure, hypertension, and stroke. Explore the statistics below to understand the impact of cardiovascular disease.






#1


Leading Cause of Death


Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States.




~1 in 3


Cardiovascular Deaths


Cardiovascular disease accounts for approximately one-third of deaths in the United States.




Every 34 Seconds


Mortality Burden


A person in the United States dies from cardiovascular disease approximately every 34 seconds.




$168 Billion+


Economic Burden


Heart disease healthcare services and medication costs exceeded $168 billion during 2021–2022.






Why Cardiovascular Health Matters


Cardiovascular disease impacts individuals, families, communities, and healthcare systems. Despite advancements in treatment and prevention, risk factors such as hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and tobacco use continue to contribute to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.


Public health interventions focused on prevention, early detection, health education, and equitable healthcare access are essential for reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease.





Major Cardiovascular Risk Factors


Select each risk factor to learn how it contributes to cardiovascular disease.





Hypertension ⌄



High blood pressure increases the workload of the heart and can damage blood vessels over time, increasing the risk of heart attack, stroke, and heart failure.

Prevention: Routine blood pressure monitoring, medication adherence, reduced sodium intake, and regular healthcare visits.




Diabetes ⌄



Elevated blood glucose levels can damage blood vessels and increase the likelihood of developing cardiovascular complications.

Prevention: Blood glucose monitoring, early screening, healthy eating, physical activity, and appropriate treatment.




Obesity ⌄



Excess body weight is associated with increased risk of hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, and cardiovascular disease.

Prevention: Supportive nutrition environments, physical activity, and access to preventive healthcare.




Smoking & Tobacco Use ⌄



Tobacco use damages blood vessels, increases blood pressure, and contributes to plaque buildup within arteries.

Prevention: Smoking cessation programs, counseling, tobacco control policies, and access to cessation resources.




Physical Inactivity ⌄



Insufficient physical activity contributes to cardiometabolic risk, including obesity, hypertension, and poor cardiovascular health.

Prevention: Safe parks, walking trails, active transportation, and community exercise opportunities.




Poor Nutrition ⌄



Diets high in sodium, saturated fat, added sugars, and processed foods may increase cardiovascular risk.

Prevention: Healthy food access, nutrition education, and policies supporting nutritious food environments.






Cardiovascular Health Disparities


Cardiovascular disease does not affect all populations equally. Explore how social and structural conditions can influence cardiovascular outcomes.




Healthcare Access


Economic Factors


Environment


Structural Factors





Healthcare Access


Limited access to primary care, preventive screenings, insurance coverage, and affordable medications can delay diagnosis and treatment. Early detection and continuity of care are important for preventing cardiovascular complications.




Economic Factors


Income, employment, housing stability, and food security influence an individual’s ability to maintain cardiovascular health. Financial barriers may limit access to nutritious foods, medications, healthcare services, and opportunities for physical activity.




Environmental Conditions


Neighborhood environments can influence cardiovascular risk through air pollution, limited access to green spaces, unsafe walking conditions, and reduced availability of healthy foods.




Structural & Social Factors


Systemic inequalities, discrimination, chronic stress, and unequal resource distribution can contribute to disparities in cardiovascular outcomes. These conditions influence health opportunities across communities and populations.






Prevention & Public Health Strategies


Cardiovascular prevention requires action at multiple levels. Select an approach to explore strategies for improving cardiovascular health.





Individual-Level Prevention


Population-Level Prevention

Monitoring cholesterol and blood glucose

Community-based cardiovascular health education


Accessible preventive healthcare services


Policies promoting healthy food environments


Tobacco control initiatives

Addressing social determinants of health


Reducing healthcare inequities







Public Health Significance


Cardiovascular disease prevention represents a critical opportunity to improve population health outcomes and reduce premature mortality. By addressing modifiable risk factors and structural barriers to healthcare, public health professionals can implement evidence-based interventions that promote healthier communities.


A population health approach emphasizes prevention, equitable access to healthcare, community engagement, health policy, and data-driven decision-making to reduce cardiovascular disease burden.

section: From Cardiovascular Data to Public Health Action
text:
From Cardiovascular Data to Public Health Action
Cardiovascular mortality disparities highlight the need for comprehensive public health strategies that prioritize prevention, early detection, treatment, and equitable access to care.
Addressing cardiovascular health requires collaboration among healthcare providers, public health professionals, policymakers, and community organizations. By implementing evidence-informed strategies at multiple levels, communities can work toward reducing preventable cardiovascular deaths and improving health outcomes.


The Public Health Approach


A systematic approach to cardiovascular health allows public health professionals to identify disparities, investigate contributing factors, develop interventions, and evaluate outcomes.



01

Define the Problem


Identify populations and communities experiencing disproportionate cardiovascular mortality.



02

Identify Risk Factors


Examine behavioral, environmental, socioeconomic, and healthcare-related contributors to cardiovascular disease.



03

Develop Solutions


Implement prevention programs, community screening, healthcare interventions, and policy strategies.



04

Evaluate & Improve


Monitor outcomes, assess effectiveness, and expand successful public health interventions.

title: Recommendations
text:
Prevention Strategies
Cardiovascular disease prevention requires interventions across multiple stages of disease progression. Primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention strategies can help reduce risk, improve early detection, and prevent complications.


PREVENTION LEVEL 01

Primary Prevention


Prevent cardiovascular disease before it develops.





♡ Heart-Healthy Nutrition


Promote access to affordable fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lower-sodium food options.




♡ Physical Activity


Encourage regular exercise through walking programs, recreation spaces, and community fitness initiatives.




♡ Tobacco Prevention


Expand tobacco prevention education and smoking cessation programs.




♡ Health Education


Improve awareness of hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol, cardiovascular risk, and prevention.




Prevention begins in the community. Community-based programs that promote healthy behaviors and improve access to resources can help reduce cardiovascular risk.




PREVENTION LEVEL 02

Secondary Prevention


Identify cardiovascular risk factors early.





♡ Blood Pressure Screening


Expand community-based blood pressure screening and referral programs.




♡ Early Detection


Increase screening for hypertension, diabetes, and high cholesterol.




♡ Mobile Health Services


Utilize mobile clinics to reach underserved and geographically isolated communities.




♡ Referral & Follow-Up


Connect individuals with abnormal screening results to primary care and appropriate treatment.




Early detection saves lives. Screening should be paired with follow-up care, referrals, and accessible treatment.




PREVENTION LEVEL 03

Tertiary Prevention


Reduce complications among individuals living with cardiovascular disease.





♡ Chronic Disease Management


Strengthen access to ongoing cardiovascular treatment and long-term disease management.




♡ Medication Access


Support medication adherence through education, affordable prescriptions, and patient assistance.




♡ Cardiac Rehabilitation


Expand access to cardiac rehabilitation and recovery services.




♡ Care Coordination


Improve communication between primary care, specialists, hospitals, and community-based services.




Continuity of care matters. Consistent treatment, follow-up, and patient support can help prevent complications and improve quality of life.



COMMUNITY & HEALTH EQUITY

Addressing the Root Causes of Cardiovascular Disparities


Cardiovascular health is influenced by more than individual behaviors. Social, economic, environmental, and structural conditions can shape access to prevention, treatment, and resources. Public health strategies should prioritize the communities experiencing the greatest burden.




Community Health Workers


Employ trusted community health workers to connect residents with screening, education, healthcare, and social resources.




Food Access & Nutrition Equity


Support food access initiatives, nutrition assistance, and healthy food availability in communities experiencing food insecurity.




Healthy Neighborhoods


Promote safe walking spaces, parks, recreation facilities, and environments that support physical activity.




Equitable Healthcare Access


Address barriers related to affordability, transportation, insurance coverage, healthcare availability, and culturally responsive care.





MONITORING & EVALUATION

How Do We Measure Progress?


Evaluating public health interventions is essential to determining whether programs effectively improve cardiovascular health outcomes. Monitoring measurable indicators can help identify successful strategies, improve program implementation, and guide future resource allocation.




Community Screening

Participation

Number of individuals screened and referred for follow-up care.




Hypertension Prevention

Blood Pressure Control

Percentage of individuals achieving controlled blood pressure.




Primary Care Access

Access & Utilization

Number of individuals connected to primary care services.




Health Education

Knowledge Improvement

Changes in cardiovascular health knowledge and awareness.




Community Initiatives

Program Reach

Participation, engagement, and retention across community programs.




Health Equity

Disparity Reduction

Changes in cardiovascular mortality disparities across populations.





THE FUTURE OF CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH

Building Stronger, Healthier Communities


Cardiovascular health is influenced by more than individual behavior. Geographic disparities, social determinants of health, healthcare access, and structural barriers all contribute to population health outcomes.


Addressing cardiovascular mortality requires a coordinated public health approach that prioritizes prevention, early detection, equitable treatment, community engagement, and evidence-informed policy.


By investing in communities and reducing barriers to care, we can move toward a future where cardiovascular health opportunities are accessible to everyone.

title: Introduction to Cardiovascular Disease
text:
♥ Stroke
A stroke occurs when blood flow to a part of the brain is interrupted or reduced—either by a blocked blood vessel (ischemic stroke) or a burst blood vessel (hemorrhagic stroke). Because brain cells are deprived of oxygen-rich blood, a stroke impacts the broader body, leading to sudden physical symptoms like paralysis, numbness, or difficulty speaking and walking.


♥ Heart Attack
A heart attack (myocardial infarction) happens when a coronary artery becomes blocked, cutting off oxygen-rich blood supply to a section of the heart muscle.The heart relies on oxygenated blood from the lungs to keep itself and the body running. When a blockage prevents the heart muscle from receiving that oxygenated blood, the tissue begins to suffer damage.


♥ Heart Failure
Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart muscle becomes too weak or too stiff to pump blood efficiently enough to meet the body’s needs. The arrow points directly from Heart Failure to the lungs because when the left side of the heart cannot pump blood out effectively, fluid backs up into the blood vessels of the lungs (pulmonary congestion), causing shortness of breath and fatigue.


♥ Aortic Aneurysm
An aortic aneurysm is an abnormal bulge or weakening in the wall of the aorta—the body’s largest artery, which carries oxygen-rich blood out of the heart.The arrow points toward the body because the aorta is the main highway delivering blood from the heart to the rest of the body; if an aneurysm ruptures or dissects, it causes life-threatening internal bleeding and cuts off systemic circulation.
